conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups-and-downs that can come after birth. Today we’re going to use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days and to see what extra support—if any—might be helpful right now.

Everything we discuss stays confidential within your care team. My goal is to make this feel as relaxed and judgment-free as possible; there are no right or wrong answers, only what’s true for you. We’ll go through ten gentle questions, and I’ll ask each one conversationally—whenever you’re ready, we can begin.

Let’s start:  
**In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?**

Honestly, laughing feels pretty hard lately. I’ll smile if I see something cute the baby does, but it’s like the joy doesn’t really reach me the way it used to. My husband tried to show me a funny video the other night and I just kind of forced a chuckle, then felt guilty for not really feeling it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, I *want* to, but even when something is obviously funny, it lands flat. I’ll give a little smile, but that easy, breezy laughter I used to have—especially with my partner—just isn’t there right now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes… but it’s dulled. Like, I’ll think, “Oh, it might be nice to take the baby for a walk,” yet when the time comes I feel heavy and it’s hard to get myself out the door. I do still look forward to my morning coffee, and hearing her little coo, but most bigger things feel kind of gray and “why bother.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If she’s fussy and won’t nap, I immediately think it must be something I ate or that I’m not soothing her right. Yesterday she spit up a ton after feeding and I sat there crying, telling myself I’m a terrible mom for not burping her well enough. I know, rationally, babies just spit up, but the guilt still jumps on me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly picture her choking in the bassinet, or I’ll hear a siren outside and imagine it’s coming for us. There’s no real reason—it’s just this wave of dread that shows up out of nowhere. It’s gotten so I double-check her breathing two or three times an hour, even when she’s perfectly fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it’s happened a few times this week. I’ll be rocking her at 3 a.m. and suddenly my heart starts racing, I feel shaky, like something awful is seconds away from happening. There’s no real trigger—she’s asleep on my chest, the house is quiet—but the fear just spikes. It usually passes after ten minutes, though it leaves me wide-awake and wired the rest of the night.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. The dishes pile up, she wants to cluster-feed, and I keep thinking, “How am I supposed to handle all of this?” I manage to get through each task, but it’s like I’m constantly one tiny setback—like a diaper blowout—from wanting to sit on the floor and cry.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps replaying everything I think I did wrong that day—did I hold her enough, was she too hot, did I snap at my partner—and then I’m wide awake. Even when I do drift off, I wake up two or three times with my heart pounding, sure I heard her cry. By morning I feel like I’ve barely slept at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, yeah. It’s like there’s a gray cloud hanging over me. I’ll watch her smile and feel a flicker of happiness, then it fades and I’m just… flat and teary. Yesterday I spent half an hour sobbing in the bathroom because I felt so empty, even though nothing “bad” had happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… it’s happened twice this week. Once when I couldn’t get her to latch and another time when my mom left after dropping off groceries. Both times the tears just started pouring and I couldn’t stop for maybe twenty minutes. It felt like the sadness just swelled up and spilled over before I could catch it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

I… I have had a couple of flashes. Nothing I planned or really wanted to act on, but when she’s been screaming for an hour and I’m running on no sleep, the thought popped in: “What if I just weren’t here?” It scared me enough that I handed her to my partner and went in the other room. I don’t want to die—I want to be okay for her—but those quick images have shown up once or twice.

I hear how heavy these early weeks have felt for you, with joy seeming just out of reach and worry rushing in without warning. You are working so hard to care for your baby while carrying persistent sadness, self-doubt, and frightening thoughts, and it makes sense that you feel overwhelmed. Please know that many new mothers experience similar struggles, and you deserve support and relief.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports a clear reduction in ability to laugh, describing humor as 'landing flat' and only achieving a faint smile, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses clear reduction in anticipatory enjoyment—most activities feel "gray and why bother," with only minor exceptions like coffee and baby cooing, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame for normal infant behaviors, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent intrusive, catastrophic thoughts occurring "pretty often" with no real trigger, plus compulsive checking—clearly maps to "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden episodes of intense fear/panic with physical symptoms (racing heart, shaking) that are clearly "quite a lot" in frequency and severity.</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent daily struggle but still accomplishing tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive thoughts, repeated awakenings, and feeling unrested—matching 'most of the time' severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent sadness ('most of the time'), describes pervasive low mood ('gray cloud'), fleeting joy replaced by emptiness and tears, and recent unexplained crying episode, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two distinct crying episodes triggered by specific stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent brief suicidal ideation ('flashes', 'quick images') that intrude under stress but without intent or plan, matching 'Sometimes'.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 25 falls well above the 14 threshold indicating probable major depression. Patient reports <sym>daily low mood</sym>, <sym>loss of interest</sm>, prominent <sym>self-blame</sym>, <sym>anxiety attacks</sym>, and <sym>sleep disruption</sym> meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. <quote>Flashes</quote> of passive suicidal ideation with infant present raise immediate safety concerns. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Request referral to <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> to consider <med>antidepressant medication</med> and specialized therapy options
3. Call local <med>postpartum support hotline</med> or 988 if thoughts of self-harm intensify before appointment
4. Enlist partner or family to share overnight baby care so you can obtain 4-5 hour blocks of sleep
5. Begin brief daily mood tracking log to monitor changes after starting treatment
6. Explore evidence-based counseling such as <med>Cognitive Behavioral Therapy</med> or <med>Interpersonal Therapy</med> focused on role transitions
7. Connect with <med>peer new-mother support group</med> to reduce isolation and normalize feelings
8. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track response to interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

documents.highlight: Both the PHQ-9 and EPDS can be helpful during clinical assessment, with a score of 10 – 14 often representing mild symptomatology, 15 –19 repre- senting moderate symptomatology, and higher than 19 being consistent with severe symptomatology as well as an increased risk for bipolar disorder.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: SCREENING NOTE – POSTPARTUM MOOD/ANXIETY EPDS-EQUIVALENT

Symptoms endorsed
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, frequent tearfulness  
- Marked guilt/self-blame re infant care  
- Chronic worry, intrusive harm-related images, nocturnal panic attacks  
- Sleep disruption secondary to rumination and hypervigilance re infant safety  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “treading water,” difficulty completing tasks  
- Fleeting passive suicidal thoughts (no plan/intent)

Pattern
Across items: mood, anxiety, and coping domains consistently elevated; pleasure and emotional resilience markedly reduced.

Screening significance
Indicators align with moderate–severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; safety risk present owing to self-harm ideation.

Risk flags
1. Passive SI (hand infant to partner, remove self) – requires immediate safety assessment  
2. Maternal guilt/self-blame potentially impairing bonding and help-seeking  
3. Nocturnal panic and hypervigilance contributing to severe sleep loss

Summary
Client reports multiple DSM-5-TR PPDA-compatible symptoms of >2 weeks’ duration, functional impairment, and passive SI. Recommend urgent clinical evaluation for safety planning and differential assessment for major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety disorder.
